gap: No result ChatGPT got states a reviewer-measured Thunderbolt transfer speed for any QNAP model. StorageReview measured the TBS-h574TX at 1,929 MB/s write and about 1,850 MB/s read from an M1 Max MacBook Pro, and said that saturated the 20 Gbps link. Club386 measured the TVS-h874T at 1.3 GB/s copying a 20 GB file from a PC. Set next to MacSources' 396/369 MB/s for an HDD-filled DXP6800 Pro on an M4 MacBook Pro, these numbers show the 20 Gbps Thunderbolt link only pays off with flash storage.
standout_why: Rival pages compared: the cited QNAP US product pages for the TVS-h674T and TVS-h874T, which give only 'maximum bandwidth of 20 Gbps' with no test conditions, and UGREEN's cited blog at ai.ugreen.com, which gives the 40 Gbps interface rate plus generic per-drive ranges (HDD 200–260 MB/s, 4-drive RAID 5 600–700 MB/s) and says it has no measured Mac results. UGREEN's Knowledge Center articles 607 and 609 load their text by script and returned nothing I could read. One chat quoted QNAP's own figure of about 1,400 MB/s for the TBS-h574TX, which is a vendor number. The ITdaily TVS-h874T review that ChatGPT got has no measured figures, and the Notebookcheck DXP6800 Pro review it got didn't test Thunderbolt. Neither StorageReview's TBS-h574TX Mac measurement nor Club386's TVS-h874T measurement appears in any of the results. Two weaker points: MacSources (DXP6800 Pro over Thunderbolt to a Mac) and Liliputing (DXP480T Plus) were both in ChatGPT's results without being cited, so those two figures are new to the answers but not to the results.
decides: This confirms the TBS-h574TX as the pick for someone who wants the direct Thunderbolt link to be fast. It is the only candidate with a named reviewer's measurement on a Mac that reaches the 20 Gbps (about 2.5 GB/s raw) ceiling: 1,929 MB/s. The all-flash DXP480T Plus came close at 1.42–1.51 GB/s (Liliputing, measured on a PC). The HDD-bay DXP6800 Pro, which ChatGPT kept recommending for capacity, measured only 396 MB/s write and 369 MB/s read on an M4 MacBook Pro with four HDDs in RAID 10 (MacSources). That is slower than its own 10GbE port, which Notebookcheck measured at 9.5 Gbit/s, about 1.19 GB/s. So for HDD arrays, Thunderbolt is a no-switch convenience, not a speed upgrade. Plain 10GbE does as well unless the pool is NVMe.
